<reason>Side A (CON) won a close, high-quality debate on the necessity arithmetic demanded by "only." A's structural case — the motion needs all three conditions to be necessary, and family unity does no work for the median single-adult transferee — survived B's best answer ("rules apply blindly; rights protect whoever they capture"), which was respectable but did not establish necessity in every case. A answered B's sharpest pressure question (why substitutes excuse work but not appeal) with a genuine functional line: destitution has substitutes in reception support, error-correction has none. A also handled the Canada trap consistently, and its closing honestly resolved B's enforceable-vs-discretionary dilemma by showing either horn defeats the work requirement's necessity. B's strongest material — the reabsorption frame, the Rwanda "no reliable remedy" line, and the delay-versus-unenforceability distinction — was effective but slightly evasive of the motion's own wording (destination-provided rights), since B's family-unity condition ended up re-located to sender-state courts. B's closing was clipped, an added execution cost roughly offsetting A's clipped first rebuttal. Both sides grounded claims in ordinary background knowledge without fake precision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's pressure question on substitutes (why can reception support excuse a missing work right but "careful first decisions" cannot excuse a missing appeal?) met by A's Rebuttal 2 functional answer — substitutes reach the interest of survival but not the interest of error-correction — followed by B's closing dilemma on whether reception support is enforceable or discretionary, which A's closing turned back: either way, work is not necessary and the motion fails.</best_rebuttal>
